column1: # title: ENG-205 Middle Ages Intro — 3 Numbers & Dates

column2: The Middle Ages run from about 450, when Roman rule in Britain collapsed, to about 1485, when Tudor rule and the Renaissance began.
Medieval English literature falls into the Anglo-Saxon period, the Anglo-Norman period after 1066, and the Middle English period of the 1300s and 1400s.
The Romans occupied Britain from AD 43 until the troops were recalled in 410, a date the notes give as about 407.
Around 450 the Anglo-Saxon conquest of Britain began.
Anglo-Saxon England was divided into seven kingdoms that had no single king until Alfred.
In 597 St. Augustine of Canterbury led a mission to Kent that spread Christianity, bringing literacy and Latin words such as "martyr" and "bishop."
Caedmon's Hymn, the earliest poem recorded in English, dates from around 658 to 680.
In 731 Bede completed the Ecclesiastical History of the English People.
Beowulf was perhaps composed around 750, though the date is uncertain.
The only surviving manuscript of Beowulf was copied around 1000.
The first Viking raids on England came around 787.
The Vikings gave English about 2,000 words, such as "give," "take," and "die."
Alfred the Great reigned from 871 to 899.
In 1066 Edward the Confessor died childless and the Witan chose Harold Godwinson as king.
In 1066 William of Normandy defeated Harold at the Battle of Hastings and became King William I.
The Norman Conquest of 1066 made French the language of power in England.
After the Norman Conquest, English absorbed about 10,000 French words.
William the Conqueror ruled England from 1066 to 1087.
William the Conqueror built 5,000 to 6,000 castles to secure Norman control of England.
After 1066 Old French served the court and law, Latin the Church and scholarship, Old English the common people, and Celtic languages such as Welsh survived at the edges.
Old English was spoken until about 1066, when the Norman Conquest pushed English below French.
Middle English re-emerged between the 1100s and the 1300s.
Geoffrey of Monmouth wrote the History of the Kings of Britain, the source of the Arthurian legends, around 1135 to 1138.
Marie de France wrote the Lais around 1165 to 1180.
In the 1300s the Alliterative Revival brought Old English-style alliterative verse back into English poetry.
During the Hundred Years' War with France, from 1337 to 1453, English gained ground as the language of power.
The Black Death struck in 1348, and the labor shortage it left behind allowed social mobility.
The Black Death of 1348 killed one quarter to one third of Europe's population.
In 1362 English was first used in the law courts and Parliament.
Julian of Norwich wrote her visionary Book of Showings between 1373 and 1393.
Sir Gawain and the Green Knight was written around 1375 to 1400.
Langland wrote the B-text of Piers Plowman between 1377 and 1379.
Around 1380 Wycliffe's followers began the first complete English Bible.
In 1381 the Peasants' Revolt briefly took control of London.
Chaucer was writing The Canterbury Tales from around 1387 to 1399.
In the 1400s a London and East Midlands form of English emerged as the standard.
In the 1400s the Great Vowel Shift moved English long vowels to new sounds.
In 1401 the first Lollards were burned as heretics.
Margery Kempe wrote The Book of Margery Kempe around 1432 to 1438.
The Wars of the Roses between the houses of Lancaster and York lasted from 1455 to 1485.
Sir Thomas Malory wrote Le Morte Darthur in prison around 1470.
In 1476 William Caxton set up England's first printing press.
In 1485 Caxton printed Malory's Morte Darthur.
In 1485 Henry VII won at Bosworth and founded the Tudor dynasty, which marks the end of the Middle Ages.
In the 1530s Henry VIII dissolved the monasteries, which had been England's main producers of books.
